title: Special teams, the third unit: how a punt gets blocked (and why kicks swung two Big Ten games)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson comes from your Penn State bet: Purdue's only points in a 14-14 first half came from a 33-yard TD pass and a blocked punt returned for a TD.

The big idea: a football team has three units. Offense, defense, and special teams: punts, kickoffs, field goals and extra points.Special teams are only about 1 snap in 6. But a single kick can be worth 7 points with no offense on the field.

White = punting team (LS long snapper, W wings, PP personal protector, P punter, G gunners). Yellow = return team (R rushers, KR returner). The yellow arrow is the free rusher; the yellow X is the block point. Numbers 1–4 match the steps below.

  1. The snap. On 4th down the long snapper (LS) fires the ball about 14 yards back to the punter (P).Snap to kick should take about 2 seconds. Any longer and the rush arrives.
  2. The protection. The linemen and two wings (W) each block one gap.The personal protector (PP), about 5 yards back, is the last blocker. He calls out the protection and takes whoever comes free.
  3. The overload. The return team puts more rushers on one side than the punting team has blockers there.If the protector picks the wrong man, one rusher runs free.
  4. The block point. Rushers don't aim at the punter. They aim about a yard in front of his kicking foot, where the ball will be.A block there sends the ball backward, often to the defense.
  5. Saturday's example. Purdue's Bisi Owens blocked Nathan Tiyce's punt and Jalil Hall scooped it and ran 31 yards for a TD: Penn State 14, Purdue 14 (StateCollege.com).Penn State's offense had been winning (it finished with 269 rushing yards). The block erased a 7-point lead in one play.
  6. The other kicks that mattered. Indiana-Minnesota: Minnesota's Luke Drzewiecki made a 60-yard field goal with 19 seconds left; Indiana's Paddy McAteer answered from 60 as time ran out (ESPN: the first FBS game in at least 30 years with two made 60-yarders). Indiana won in overtime.Penn State's Ryan Barker missed from 55. Last week, Oregon missed three field goals in a loss at Illinois.

How to log it in your drill: on 4th down, first check the formation. A punter 14 yards deep with a personal protector in front of him is a punt, so there's nothing to call. But watch for a fake punt: a direct snap to the protector, or the punter running. Teams fake most on 4th-and-short near midfield, when the return team only has one man deep. Log a fake as RUN (a direct snap) or PASS (the punter throws).

Why it matters for your bets: special-teams TDs, blocked kicks and long field goals are points the offense didn't earn. Totals and margins can't predict them. Purdue's block helped keep your Penn State bet alive at halftime (21-14). The two 60-yarders pushed Indiana-Minnesota into overtime. In today's Chiefs-Broncos Under, the altitude in Denver makes long field goals easier, so drives that stall at the 40 can still score 3.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): today, Chiefs at Broncos (1:25 p.m., CBS): field goals at altitude. Ravens at Bills (10:00 a.m., CBS). Monday, Bears at Seahawks (5:15 p.m., ESPN). Next Saturday, Penn State at Washington: does Penn State's punt protection hold up?

Video: search YouTube for "punt protection explained," "how to block a punt," and "fake punt personal protector."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: On a punt, who is the last blocker standing in front of the punter?
quiz.w: The personal protector (PP) lines up about 5 yards back, calls the protection and picks up the rusher who comes free.

o: About a yard in front of the punter's kicking foot
quiz.w: That's the block point: where the ball will be when it's kicked. Aiming at the punter usually means a roughing penalty.

quiz.q: What is an "overload" on a punt rush?
o: Putting more rushers on one side than there are blockers
Kicking the ball out of bounds
A penalty for too many players
quiz.w: More rushers than blockers on one side means someone runs free if the protector guesses wrong. That's how Purdue got to Penn State's punt.

quiz.q: It's 4th-and-1 at midfield. The ball is snapped directly to the personal protector, who runs up the middle. How do you log it?
quiz.w: A direct snap to the protector who runs is a fake punt run. Teams try it most on 4th-and-short near midfield.
